topic: Units, prefixes and basic electrical quantities

notes.front: What is an electron, in one sentence?
notes.back: A tiny particle with a negative electric charge, found in all matter; in metals, many electrons are free to move.
notes.explanation: Electric current is the movement of electrons, so the next cards on current, conductors and insulators build on them.
notes.example: Silver, copper, gold and aluminium have many free electrons, which is why they are good conductors.
notes.source: US Navy, NEETS Module 1 (NAVEDTRA 14173), Introduction to Matter, Energy, and Direct Current, pp. 1-4, 1-8; NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T5A07, T5A03

notes.front: What is an electric circuit, in one sentence?
notes.back: A complete path for electric current, such as a battery, wires and a lamp joined in a loop, so electrons go out and back.
notes.explanation: With no complete path there is no current, so every question about current, voltage and components assumes a circuit.
notes.example: A torch: its batteries, switch and bulb form one loop; opening the switch breaks the path and the bulb goes out.
notes.source: US Navy, NEETS Module 1 (NAVEDTRA 14173), Introduction to Matter, Energy, and Direct Current, pp. 3-2, 3-19, Appendix I (“Circuit”); NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T5A03

notes.front: What is electrical current, in one sentence?
notes.back: The flow of electrons in an electric circuit.
notes.explanation: Almost everything in radio is about making, controlling or measuring this flow. It is measured in amperes.
notes.example: Like the amount of water flowing along a pipe each second.

notes.front: What is voltage, in one sentence?
notes.back: Electric potential: a difference in voltage between two points is what causes electrons to flow.
notes.explanation: No voltage difference, no current. Voltage is stated in volts and measured with a voltmeter.
notes.example: Like the difference in water pressure between the two ends of a pipe, which is what makes the water move.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T5A05, T7D01, T5B03

notes.front: What is electrical power, in one sentence?
notes.back: The rate at which electrical energy is used, measured in watts.
notes.explanation: Transmitter output and the legal power limits are both stated in watts, so this unit comes up constantly.
notes.example: A 100-watt lamp uses energy twice as fast as a 50-watt lamp.

notes.front: What is an electrical conductor, in one sentence?
notes.back: A material that current flows through easily; metals are good conductors because they have many free electrons.
notes.explanation: Current is a flow of electrons, so a material with many free electrons carries it well.
notes.example: The metal wire inside a cable is the conductor.

notes.front: What is an electrical insulator, in one sentence?
notes.back: A material that current does not flow through easily, such as glass.
notes.explanation: Conductors carry current where it should go; insulators keep it from going anywhere else.
notes.example: If a conductor is an open water pipe, an insulator is a closed valve.

notes.front: What is alternating current, in one sentence?
notes.back: Current that alternates between positive and negative directions.
notes.explanation: Its direction keeps reversing, over and over. How many complete cycles it makes each second is its frequency.
notes.example: Like a saw moving back and forth, rather than a wheel turning one way.

notes.front: What is direct current (DC), in one sentence?
notes.back: Current that flows in one direction only; a battery supplies it.
notes.explanation: It is the opposite of alternating current, whose direction keeps reversing. The pool writes it “direct current” or “DC”.
notes.example: A battery-powered torch runs on direct current: it flows one way round the circuit.
notes.source: US Navy, NEETS Module 1 (NAVEDTRA 14173), Introduction to Matter, Energy, and Direct Current, Appendix I (“Direct current”), p. 3-34; NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T5A11

notes.front: What is frequency, in one sentence?
notes.back: The number of times per second that an alternating current makes a complete cycle, measured in hertz.
notes.explanation: Radio bands and channels are all identified by frequency, so it is the number you will use most.
notes.example: A current that completes 1000 cycles every second has a frequency of 1000 hertz.

notes.front: What is resistance, in one sentence?
notes.back: Opposition to the flow of current, measured in ohms.
notes.explanation: Resistance opposes every kind of current, direct and alternating alike, whatever its frequency.
notes.example: Like a narrow section of pipe that holds back the flow of water.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T5A11, T6A01, T5D04

notes.front: What are metric prefixes, in one sentence?
notes.back: Word parts that multiply or divide a unit; on this exam they go in steps of 1000 (kilo × 1000, milli ÷ 1000), except pico.
notes.explanation: Radio quantities range from millionths of a volt to billions of hertz, so the exam expects quick conversions. Pico is the exception: it is a millionth of micro, not a thousandth.
notes.example: 1 kilovolt is 1000 volts; 1500 milliamperes is 1.5 amperes.

notes.front: What is RF (radio frequency), in one sentence?
notes.back: The frequencies used for radio: below 3000 GHz by the rules’ definition, or 3 kHz to 300 GHz in the US Navy’s training course.
notes.explanation: Definitions differ at the edges, which is why the two figures differ; both put every amateur band inside the range. The pool uses “RF” constantly: RF current, RF power, RF exposure.
notes.example: A 146 MHz signal is RF; a 1 kHz audio tone is below the 3 kHz bottom of the range.
notes.source: 47 CFR 2.1 (“Radio Waves or Hertzian Waves”); US Navy, NEETS Module 10 (NAVEDTRA 14182), p. 2-7 and Appendix I

notes.front: What are decibels (dB), in one sentence?
notes.back: A way of stating a change in power as a ratio: +3 dB is about double, −3 dB about half, +10 dB ten times.
notes.explanation: Decibels describe the ratio, not the amount: 5 W to 10 W and 50 W to 100 W are both +3 dB.
notes.example: Going from 20 watts to 200 watts is ten times the power, so it is +10 dB.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T5B09, T5B11; 47 CFR 97.313(f) (half-power = −3 dB)

image.alt: A ladder of decibel values: +10 dB is ×10 (20 W to 200 W), +6 dB is ×4, +3 dB is ×2 (5 W to 10 W), 0 dB is no change, −3 dB is half, −6 dB is a quarter (12 W to 3 W).
image.credit: Drawn for this deck from NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool T5B09–T5B11

notes.front: What is an electric field, in one sentence?
notes.back: The space around electrically charged particles, such as electrons, in which they push or pull on other charges.
notes.explanation: Capacitance, next, is energy stored in an electric field, and every radio wave carries one.
notes.example: Two electrons push each other away through their electric fields, because like charges repel.
notes.source: US Navy, NEETS Module 1 (NAVEDTRA 14173), Introduction to Matter, Energy, and Direct Current, pp. 1-11, 1-12; NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T5C01, T3B03

notes.front: What is a magnetic field, in one sentence?
notes.back: The magnetic influence present in the space around a magnet or around a wire carrying current.
notes.explanation: Inductance is energy stored in a magnetic field, and every radio wave has one at right angles to its electric field.
notes.example: A compass needle placed next to a wire carrying current swings round to point at right angles to the wire, because the current makes a magnetic field.
notes.source: US Navy, NEETS Module 1 (NAVEDTRA 14173), Introduction to Matter, Energy, and Direct Current, p. 1-52; US Navy, NEETS Module 2 (NAVEDTRA 14174), chapter 1; NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T5C03, T3B01, T3B03

notes.front: What is capacitance, in one sentence?
notes.back: The ability to store energy in an electric field, measured in farads.
notes.explanation: Capacitors are the components built to do this; you will meet them with the other components.
notes.example: Like a tank that stores water under pressure, ready to release it.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T5C01, T5C02, T6A04

notes.front: What is inductance, in one sentence?
notes.back: The ability to store energy in a magnetic field, measured in henrys.
notes.explanation: It is the magnetic-field counterpart of capacitance, which stores energy in an electric field. Inductors are built to do it.
notes.example: Like a heavy flywheel that stores energy in its motion and keeps turning.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T5C03, T5C04, T6A06

notes.front: What is impedance, in one sentence?
notes.back: The opposition to alternating current flow, measured in ohms.
notes.explanation: It uses the same unit as resistance, the ohm, but is the term for opposition to alternating current.
notes.example: Like resistance, but for current that keeps reversing direction.

notes.front: In what unit is electrical current measured?
notes.explanation: Current is the flow of electrons; the ampere measures how much flows.

notes.front: In what unit is voltage stated, and which instrument measures it?
notes.explanation: A voltmeter measures electric potential, which is voltage. One kilovolt is 1000 volts.

notes.front: In what unit is electrical power measured?
notes.explanation: Power is the rate of using energy. Watt-hours multiply power by time (1 watt used for 1 hour), so they measure an amount of energy, not a rate.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T5A02; US Navy, NEETS Module 1 (NAVEDTRA 14173), Introduction to Matter, Energy, and Direct Current, p. 3-18

notes.front: What is the unit of frequency?
notes.explanation: One hertz is one complete cycle per second. The rules abbreviate it Hz.

notes.front: Why are metals generally good conductors of electricity?
notes.explanation: Current is a flow of electrons, so free electrons are what carry it.

notes.front: Between which directions does alternating current alternate?
notes.explanation: It does not just pulse between one direction and zero; it reverses fully, from positive to negative and back.

notes.front: Which kinds of current does resistance oppose?
notes.back: All of them: direct, alternating and RF current.
notes.explanation: Resistance is opposition to current of any kind, which is why the pool keys "All these choices are correct".

notes.front: What is the unit of capacitance?
notes.explanation: Capacitance is stored energy in an electric field; farads measure how much.

notes.front: What is the unit of inductance?
notes.explanation: Inductance is stored energy in a magnetic field; henrys measure how much.

notes.front: What is the unit of impedance?
notes.explanation: Impedance shares its unit with resistance: both are oppositions to current.

notes.front: The prefix kilo means {{c1::× 1000}}: one kilovolt is one thousand volts.
notes.explanation: So 1500 kilohertz is 1,500,000 hertz.

notes.front: The prefix mega means {{c1::× 1,000,000}} (1000 kilo): 28.400 megahertz is 28,400 kilohertz.
notes.explanation: Each step from kilo to mega is another × 1000.

notes.front: The prefix giga means {{c1::1000 mega}}: 2425 megahertz is 2.425 gigahertz.
notes.explanation: Giga is the next step up from mega, another × 1000.

notes.front: The prefix milli means {{c1::÷ 1000 (one-thousandth)}}: 500 milliwatts is 0.5 watts.
notes.explanation: So 3000 milliamperes is 3 amperes and 1.5 amperes is 1500 milliamperes.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T5B05, T5B06, T5B01

notes.front: The prefix micro means {{c1::one-millionth}}: one microvolt is one-millionth of a volt.
notes.explanation: Micro is 1000 times smaller than milli.

notes.front: The prefix pico means {{c1::one-millionth of micro}}: 1,000,000 picofarads is 1 microfarad.
notes.explanation: Pico is the smallest prefix in the exam; it appears with capacitance in farads.

notes.front: When converting megahertz to kilohertz, what do you multiply by?
notes.explanation: Each prefix step (giga, mega, kilo, unit) is × 1000 going down and ÷ 1000 going up: 3.525 MHz is 3525 kHz.

notes.front: How is kilohertz abbreviated, exactly?
notes.back: kHz: small k, capital H, small z.
notes.explanation: Only this capitalisation is correct; KHz, khz and KHZ are the wrong options in the pool.

notes.front: How is megahertz abbreviated, exactly?
notes.back: MHz: capital M, capital H, small z.
notes.explanation: Only this capitalisation is correct; mHz, mHZ and Mhz are the wrong options in the pool.

notes.front: About how many decibels is a doubling of power?
notes.explanation: Going from 5 watts to 10 watts is a doubling, closest to 3 dB. A halving is about −3 dB.

notes.front: How many decibels is a tenfold increase in power?
notes.explanation: Going from 20 watts to 200 watts multiplies power by ten: +10 dB.

notes.front: About how many decibels is a drop to one quarter of the power?
notes.explanation: A quarter is two halvings, and each halving is about −3 dB: 12 W to 6 W to 3 W.

notes.front: Electrical current is measured in which of the following units?
notes.choices:
A) Volts
B) Watts
C) Ohms
D) Amperes
notes.choicesExplained: A: volts measure voltage. B: watts measure power. C: ohms measure resistance and impedance.
notes.explanation: The ampere counts how fast charge flows: 1 ampere is 1 coulomb of charge passing a point each second.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T5A01; US Navy, NEETS Module 1 (NAVEDTRA 14173), p. 1-59

notes.front: Electrical power is measured in which of the following units?
notes.choices:
A) Volts
B) Watts
C) Watt-hours
D) Amperes
notes.choicesExplained: A: volts measure voltage. C: watt-hours multiply power by time, so they measure an amount of energy, not a rate. D: amperes measure current.
notes.explanation: Power is how fast energy is used. Multiply watts by hours and you get an amount of energy, in watt-hours, which is why watt-hours cannot be the unit of power.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T5A02; US Navy, NEETS Module 1 (NAVEDTRA 14173), p. 3-18

notes.front: What is the term for the flow of electrons in an electric circuit?
notes.choices:
A) Voltage
B) Amperes per second
C) Volts per second
D) Current
notes.choicesExplained: A: voltage is what causes the flow, not the flow itself. B, C: these are not the name of the flow; current is measured in amperes.
notes.explanation: Electron movement through a conductor is what is called an electric current. Voltage is the push that causes it, so the flow and the push are different things.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T5A03; US Navy, NEETS Module 1 (NAVEDTRA 14173), p. 1-8

notes.front: What term describes the number of times per second that an alternating current makes a complete cycle?
notes.choices:
A) Pulse rate
B) Wave number
C) Frequency
D) Wavelength
notes.choicesExplained: A, B: pulse rate and wave number name other quantities; the pool’s term for cycles per second is frequency. D: wavelength is a length, not a count of cycles.
notes.explanation: Frequency counts complete cycles each second, and its unit, the hertz, is one cycle per second: house current that makes 60 cycles a second is 60 hertz.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T5A04; US Navy, NEETS Module 10 (NAVEDTRA 14182), p. 2-7

notes.front: A difference in which of the following causes electron flow?
notes.choices:
A) Voltage
B) Ampere-hours
C) Capacitance
D) Inductance
notes.choicesExplained: B: an ampere-hour is current multiplied by time, as in a battery’s capacity rating; it is not a difference that drives electrons. C: capacitance is stored energy in an electric field. D: inductance is stored energy in a magnetic field.
notes.explanation: A difference in voltage (electric potential) between two points is what makes electrons flow.

notes.front: What is the unit of frequency?
notes.choices:
A) Hertz
B) Henry
C) Farad
D) Epicycles per second
notes.choicesExplained: B: the henry is the unit of inductance. C: the farad is the unit of capacitance. D: not a real unit.
notes.explanation: One hertz is one complete cycle per second. The henry and the farad sound similar but are the units of inductance and capacitance.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T5A06; US Navy, NEETS Module 10 (NAVEDTRA 14182), p. 2-7

notes.front: Why are metals generally good conductors of electricity?
notes.choices:
A) They have relatively high density
B) They have many free electrons
C) They have many free protons
D) They have relatively high Young’s modulus values
notes.choicesExplained: A, D: how well a material conducts depends on its atomic structure, which gives metals many free electrons, not on its density or its Young’s modulus. C: protons are not what flows; current is a flow of electrons.
notes.explanation: Many free electrons are available to move, and current is a flow of electrons.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T5A07; US Navy, NEETS Module 1 (NAVEDTRA 14173), Introduction to Matter, Energy, and Direct Current, p. 1-8

notes.front: Which of the following is a good electrical insulator?
notes.choices:
A) Sea water
B) Glass
C) Stainless steel
D) Graphite
notes.choicesExplained: A, C, D: sea water, stainless steel and graphite all let current flow; only glass is a good insulator. Stainless steel, like other metals, has many free electrons.
notes.explanation: Glass does not let current flow easily, so it is a good insulator.

notes.front: Which of the following describes alternating current?
notes.back: Current that alternates between positive and negative directions
notes.choices:
A) Current that alternates between a positive direction and zero
B) Current that alternates between a negative direction and zero
C) Current that alternates between positive and negative directions
D) All these answers are correct
notes.choicesExplained: A, B: alternating current does not stop at zero in one direction; it swings fully to the other direction. D: only C is correct.
notes.explanation: Alternating current reverses fully, between positive and negative directions.

notes.front: Which term describes the rate at which electrical energy is used?
notes.choices:
A) Resistance
B) Current
C) Power
D) Voltage
notes.choicesExplained: A: resistance opposes current. B: current is the flow of electrons. D: voltage causes the flow.
notes.explanation: Energy is an amount; power is how fast it is used. That is why 1 watt of power used for 1 hour makes a separate unit of energy, the watt-hour.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T5A10; US Navy, NEETS Module 1 (NAVEDTRA 14173), p. 3-18

notes.front: What type of current flow is opposed by resistance?
notes.choices:
A) Direct current
B) Alternating current
C) RF current
D) All these choices are correct
notes.choicesExplained: A, B, C: each is opposed by resistance, so picking only one is incomplete.
notes.explanation: Resistance is opposition to the flow of current, and direct, alternating and RF current are all flows of electrons, so all three are opposed.

notes.front: How many milliamperes is 1.5 amperes?
notes.choices:
A) 0.0000015 milliamperes
B) 0.0015 milliamperes
C) 1500 milliamperes
D) 1,500,000 milliamperes
notes.choicesExplained: A, B: these divide instead of multiply. D: multiplies by a million, not a thousand.
notes.explanation: Milli means one-thousandth, so 1.5 amperes × 1000 = 1500 milliamperes.

notes.front: Which is equal to 1,500,000 hertz?
notes.choices:
A) 1500 kHz
B) 1500 MHz
C) 15 GHz
D) 150 kHz
notes.choicesExplained: B: 1500 MHz is 1,500,000,000 Hz. C: 15 GHz is far larger still. D: 150 kHz is only 150,000 Hz.

notes.front: Which is equal to one kilovolt?
notes.choices:
A) One one-thousandth of a volt
B) One hundred volts
C) One thousand volts
D) One million volts
notes.choicesExplained: A: that is a millivolt. B: a kilovolt is 1000, not 100. D: that is a megavolt.
notes.explanation: Kilo means × 1000, so one kilovolt is 1000 volts.

notes.front: Which is equal to one microvolt?
notes.choices:
A) One one-millionth of a volt
B) One million volts
C) One thousand kilovolts
D) One one-thousandth of a volt
notes.choicesExplained: B, C: these are huge, not tiny. D: one-thousandth of a volt is a millivolt.
notes.explanation: Micro means one-millionth and milli one-thousandth, so a microvolt is a thousand times smaller than a millivolt.

notes.front: Which is equal to 500 milliwatts?
notes.choices:
A) 5 watts
B) 0.5 watts
C) 500,000 watts
D) 500,000,000 watts
notes.choicesExplained: A: 5 watts would be 5000 milliwatts. C, D: these multiply instead of divide.
notes.explanation: Milli means one-thousandth: 500 ÷ 1000 = 0.5 watts.

notes.front: Which is equal to 3000 milliamperes?
notes.choices:
A) 0.003 amperes
B) 0.3 amperes
C) 3,000,000 amperes
D) 3 amperes
notes.choicesExplained: A: 0.003 amperes is 3 milliamperes. B: 0.3 amperes is 300 milliamperes. C: multiplies instead of divides.
notes.explanation: Milli means one-thousandth, so 1000 milliamperes make 1 ampere, and 3000 milliamperes make 3 amperes.

notes.front: Which is equal to 3.525 MHz?
notes.choicesExplained: A, B: these divide instead of multiply. D: multiplies by a million instead of a thousand.
notes.explanation: One megahertz is 1000 kilohertz, so 3.525 × 1000 = 3525 kHz.

notes.front: Which is equal to 1,000,000 picofarads?
notes.choices:
A) 0.001 microfarads
B) 1 microfarad
C) 1000 microfarads
D) 1,000,000,000 microfarads
notes.choicesExplained: A: that would be 1000 picofarads. C, D: far too large.
notes.explanation: Pico is one-millionth of micro, so a million picofarads make one microfarad.

notes.front: Which decibel value most closely represents a power increase from 5 watts to 10 watts?
notes.choices:
A) 2 dB
B) 3 dB
C) 5 dB
D) 10 dB
notes.choicesExplained: A: too small for a doubling. C: about three times the power. D: ten times the power.
notes.explanation: Each 3 dB is about a doubling of power, and 5 W to 10 W is exactly double.

notes.front: Which decibel value most closely represents a power decrease from 12 watts to 3 watts?
notes.choices:
A) -1 dB
B) -3 dB
C) -6 dB
D) -9 dB
notes.choicesExplained: A: a much smaller change. B: −3 dB is only half (12 W to 6 W). D: −9 dB is an eighth (12 W to 1.5 W).
notes.explanation: 12 W to 3 W is a quarter: two halvings of about −3 dB each, so −6 dB.

notes.front: Which decibel value represents a power increase from 20 watts to 200 watts?
notes.choices:
A) 10 dB
B) 12 dB
C) 18 dB
D) 28 dB
notes.choicesExplained: B, C, D: each is more than a tenfold increase.
notes.explanation: 20 W to 200 W is ten times the power, which is exactly 10 dB.

notes.front: Which is equal to 28400 kHz?
notes.choicesExplained: A: the number was divided but the unit was left as kHz. B, C: misplaced decimal points.
notes.explanation: Divide kilohertz by 1000 to get megahertz: 28400 ÷ 1000 = 28.400 MHz.

notes.front: Which is equal to 2425 MHz?
notes.choicesExplained: A: divides by a million instead of a thousand. B, D: misplaced decimal points.
notes.explanation: Divide megahertz by 1000 to get gigahertz: 2425 ÷ 1000 = 2.425 GHz.

notes.front: What describes the ability to store energy in an electric field?
notes.choices:
A) Inductance
B) Resistance
C) Frequency
D) Capacitance
notes.choicesExplained: A: inductance stores energy in a magnetic field. B: resistance opposes current. C: frequency counts cycles per second.
notes.explanation: Capacitance and inductance are the pair to keep apart: capacitance goes with the electric field (unit: farad), inductance with the magnetic field (unit: henry).
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T5C01, T5C02, T5C03, T5C04

notes.front: What is the unit of capacitance?
notes.choices:
A) Farad
B) Ohm
C) Volt
D) Henry
notes.choicesExplained: B: the ohm measures resistance and impedance. C: the volt measures voltage. D: the henry measures inductance.
notes.explanation: Capacitance goes with the electric field and the farad; its magnetic-field partner, inductance, goes with the henry, which is why those two options are easily swapped.

notes.front: What describes the ability to store energy in a magnetic field?
notes.choices:
A) Admittance
B) Capacitance
C) Resistance
D) Inductance
notes.choicesExplained: A: the pool’s term for storing energy in a magnetic field is inductance, not admittance. B: capacitance stores energy in an electric field. C: resistance opposes current.
notes.explanation: Inductance and capacitance are the pair to keep apart: inductance goes with the magnetic field (unit: henry), capacitance with the electric field (unit: farad).
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T5C03, T5C01, T5C02, T5C04

notes.front: What is the unit of inductance?
notes.choices:
A) Coulomb
B) Farad
C) Henry
D) Ohm
notes.choicesExplained: A: the coulomb is the unit of electric charge. B: the farad measures capacitance. D: the ohm measures resistance and impedance.
notes.explanation: Inductance goes with the magnetic field and the henry; its electric-field partner, capacitance, goes with the farad, which is why those two options are easily swapped.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T5C04; US Navy, NEETS Module 1 (NAVEDTRA 14173), Introduction to Matter, Energy, and Direct Current, p. 1-55; NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T5C02

notes.front: What is the unit of impedance?
notes.choices:
A) Volt
B) Ampere
C) Coulomb
D) Ohm
notes.choicesExplained: A: the volt measures voltage. B: the ampere measures current. C: the coulomb is the unit of electric charge.
notes.explanation: Impedance, like resistance, is an opposition to current, so both are measured in the same unit, the ohm.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T5C05; US Navy, NEETS Module 1 (NAVEDTRA 14173), Introduction to Matter, Energy, and Direct Current, p. 1-55

notes.front: What is the abbreviation for kilohertz?
notes.choices:
A) kHz
B) khz
C) KHz
D) KHZ
notes.choicesExplained: B, C, D: wrong capitalisation; only small k, capital H, small z is correct.
notes.explanation: The correct abbreviation for kilohertz is kHz.

notes.front: What is the abbreviation for megahertz?
notes.choices:
A) mHz
B) mHZ
C) Mhz
D) MHz
notes.choicesExplained: A, B, C: wrong capitalisation; only capital M, capital H, small z is correct.
notes.explanation: The correct abbreviation for megahertz is MHz.

notes.front: What is impedance?
notes.back: The opposition to AC current flow
notes.choices:
A) The opposition to AC current flow
B) The inverse of resistance
C) The inverse of reactance
D) The power handling capability of a component
notes.choicesExplained: B, C: impedance is itself an opposition to current, not the inverse of resistance or of reactance (the opposition that coils and capacitors offer to AC). D: not a power rating.
notes.explanation: Impedance is the total opposition to alternating current: it can combine resistance and the reactance of coils and capacitors, and it is measured in ohms.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T5C12; US Navy, NEETS Module 2 (NAVEDTRA 14174), Appendix I (“Impedance”, “Inductive reactance”, “Capacitive reactance”)

notes.front: Which instrument would you use to measure electric potential?
notes.choices:
A) An ammeter
B) A voltmeter
C) A potentiometer
D) An ohmmeter
notes.choicesExplained: A: an ammeter measures current. C: a potentiometer is a component often used as an adjustable volume control. D: an ohmmeter measures resistance.
notes.explanation: Electric potential difference is voltage, the push that makes electrons flow, so it is measured with a voltmeter; the ammeter measures the resulting current.

notes.front: Capacitance or inductance: which stores energy in a magnetic field, and what is its unit?
notes.back: Inductance, measured in henrys. Capacitance stores energy in an electric field, in farads.
notes.explanation: The two are easily swapped: capacitance goes with the electric field and farads, inductance with the magnetic field and henrys.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T5C01, T5C02, T5C03, T5C04

notes.front: Resistance or impedance: which is the term for opposition to alternating current specifically?
notes.back: Impedance. Resistance opposes all current; both are measured in ohms.
notes.explanation: Same unit, different scope: impedance is defined for alternating current, resistance for any current.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T5C12, T5A11, T5C05

notes.front: Current or voltage: which is the flow of electrons, and which causes it?
notes.back: Current is the flow; a difference in voltage causes it.
notes.explanation: Measured differently too: current in amperes with an ammeter, voltage in volts with a voltmeter.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T5A03, T5A05, T7D01, T7D04

notes.front: Milli or micro: which means one-millionth?
notes.explanation: A millivolt is a thousandth of a volt; a microvolt is a millionth, 1000 times smaller again.

notes.front: Which is ten times the power, +3 dB or +10 dB?
notes.back: +10 dB. +3 dB is only about double.
notes.explanation: Mixing these up is the classic decibel error: 5 W to 10 W is +3 dB; 20 W to 200 W is +10 dB.
